questions.problem: Find the angle between $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 4+(-6)\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-6)^{2}}\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{37}\cdot \sqrt{17}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{629}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{629}})≈{94.6}^{∘}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $P$, $Q$, $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨-3,0,-1⟩,\,q=⟨-1,1,0⟩,\,r=⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠PQR=\theta .$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/209d43a5aab5d57fbd4cd7b421d41f0fa85bc58cfdd36251a8acf392b0ba7312.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{QP}$ and $\overset{\to }{QR}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{QP} & =p-q \\  & =⟨-3,0,-1⟩-⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{QR} & =r-q \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩-⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{QP}$ and $\overset{\to }{QR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{QP}\cdot \overset{\to }{QR}}{|\overset{\to }{QP}||\overset{\to }{QR}|} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-6}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-1)={180}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Find $∠BAC$ given the points $A(2,-1,1)$, $B(3,1,-2)$, and $C(-1,1,1).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,-1,1⟩,\,b=⟨3,1,-2⟩,\,c=⟨-1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3,1,-2⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨-1,1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}})≈{86}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Find $∠QPR$ given the points $P(2,1,2)$, $Q(1,3,2)$, and $R(4,5,-2).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $P$, $Q$, $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨2,1,2⟩,\,q=⟨1,3,2⟩,\,r=⟨4,5,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠QPR=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/3003f0cb329a8f8ef9bc315c70df4773ac1f0c54843dea1208c68bd0f6227bd1.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =⟨1,3,2⟩-⟨2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,2,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =⟨4,5,-2⟩-⟨2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,4,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot \overset{\to }{PR}}{|\overset{\to }{PQ}||\overset{\to }{PR}|} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 2+2\cdot 4+0\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{6}{6\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5})≈{63}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the points $D(1,3,2)$, $E(t,2,4)$ and $F(3,t,3).$ Find $∠EDF$ given that $\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}=2.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $D$, $E$, $F$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}d=⟨1,\,3,\,2⟩,\,e=⟨t,\,2,\,4⟩,\,f=⟨3,\,t,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△DEF$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠EDF=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/c9cfb3e84e6f76d243125f2a09246b2a1300a0134e71359bb2b528082f064f93.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{DE}$ and $\overset{\to }{DF}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =e-d \\  & =⟨t,\,2,\,4⟩-⟨1,\,3,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨t-1,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{DF} & =f-d \\  & =⟨3,\,t,\,3⟩-⟨1,\,3,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,t-3,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}=2$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF} & =2 \\ (t-1)\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot (t-3)+2\cdot 1 & =2 \\ 2t-2-t+3+2 & =2 \\ t & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =⟨-1-1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-1,2⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{DF} & =⟨2,-1-3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-4,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{DE}$ and $\overset{\to }{DF}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}}{|\overset{\to }{DE}||\overset{\to }{DF}|} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{9}\cdot \sqrt{21}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3\sqrt{21}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{3\sqrt{21}})≈{81.64}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Given that $c\cdot d=11$, find the angle between $c=⟨2t,1⟩$ and $d=⟨2,3⟩.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $c\cdot d=11$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot d & =11 \\ 2t\cdot 2+1\cdot 3 & =11 \\ 4t+3 & =11 \\ 4t & =8 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =⟨2(2),1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $c$ and $d$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,c\,||\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}}{\sqrt{{c}_{x}^{2}+{c}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{17}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}})≈{42.27}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the points $A(3t,t,4),$ $B(3t,4t,3)$ and $C(5t,t+1,5).$ Find $∠BAC$ given that $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2.$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,$ $B$ and $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩,\,b=⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩,\,c=⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,3t,\,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2$, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC} & =2 \\ 0\cdot 2t+3t\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1 & =2 \\ 3t-1 & =2 \\ 3t & =3 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,3,-1⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨2,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{2}{2\sqrt{15}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}})≈{75}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Given that $a\cdot b=-5$, find the angle between $a=⟨2t,t⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $a\cdot b=-5$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =-5 \\ 2t\cdot 1+t\cdot 3 & =-5 \\ 2t+3t & =-5 \\ 5t & =-5 \\ t & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨2(-1),\,(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $a$ and $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{10}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})={135}^{∘}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =11 \\ t\cdot (-4)+(t-1)\cdot (-1) & =11 \\ -4t-t+1 & =11 \\ -5t & =10 \\ t & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨(-2),(-2)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $p$ and $q$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,||\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\cdot \sqrt{17}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}})≈{42.3}^{∘}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Their Components
canonical_examples.problem: Find the angle between $\mathbf{a}=\langle 2,-1,1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 1,5,-2 \rangle$. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 5+1\cdot (-2)}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{6} \right) \approx 111.9^\circ.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
canonical_examples.problem: Find $\angle BAC$ given the points $A(2,-1,-5)$, $B(-1,0,-4)$, and $C(5,1,1).$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,-1,-5⟩,\,b=⟨-1,0,-4⟩,\,c=⟨5,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $\triangle ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $\angle BAC = \theta.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14045824/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨-1,0,-4⟩-⟨2,-1,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨5,1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨3,2,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{-3\cdot 3+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 6}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-1}{\sqrt{11}\sqrt{49}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{7\sqrt{11}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{1}{7\sqrt{11}} \right) \approx 92.5^\circ.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given the Value of Their Dot Product
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=-4$, find the angle between $\mathbf{a}=\langle t, \, -2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 6, \, t \rangle$. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, since $\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=-4$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =-4 \\ t\cdot 6+(-2)\cdot t & =-4 \\ 6t-2t & =-4 \\ 4t & =-4 \\ t & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨-1,-2⟩,\,b=⟨6,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{37}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{185}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{185}} \right) \approx 107.1^\circ.
$$
